name: Parallax Titan
specific_features: Apparent positional shift when viewed from different angles exceeding calculated parallax
description: Parallax Titan is a gas giant of considerable mass whose most unsettling property is visual: the planet appears to shift position relative to background stars by an amount significantly greater than its actual parallax should produce. The effect is subtle but measurable, as if the planet occupies a slightly different position in space depending on the observer's location. Its cloud layers descend in stratified bands for over five hundred kilometers, each layer a different chemical composition and color, creating a banded appearance of cream, ochre, and deep brown.

The hexagonal polar vortex is the planet's most visually distinctive feature, a precisely six-sided storm pattern at the north pole that has persisted for as long as the planet has been observed. Deep convection columns drive material from the lower atmosphere to the cloud tops in periodic upwellings that briefly expose warmer, differently colored gases from below. The atmosphere smells of ammonia and methane in the upper layers, shifting to hydrogen sulfide in the depths.

Microbial life has been detected in the mid-atmosphere, floating in the temperate zone between the frigid cloud tops and the crushing depths below. These organisms are gas-phase life, existing as complex chemical systems suspended in the atmospheric medium without any solid substrate. Their discovery challenged fundamental assumptions about the requirements for life and opened entirely new branches of biology.

The anomalous parallax effect remains the planet's deepest mystery, with theories ranging from gravitational lensing by an unseen mass to spatial distortion caused by the planet's intense magnetic field. Navigation in the system requires constant positional correction, as sensor readings consistently place the planet in a slightly wrong location. The gas-phase microbes have become a major research focus, with atmospheric sampling stations operating at multiple altitudes.
